text:
maria: quick sanity check — aborting a streaming call in node sometimes still fires the auth refresh flow (we rotate refresh tokens). i see duplicate token exchanges after abort. anyone else seen this?

jon: seen something similar in prod last month. usually tied to our oauth lib retrying on 401 and not being cancelled. what SDK + auth lib are you using?

maria: node sdk v0.24.1, our oauth helper is a tiny wrapper around simple-oauth2. we call fetch with AbortController. example: 
```js
const ac = new AbortController();
fetch(streamUrl, { signal: ac.signal, headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${access}` } })
// on client cancel
ac.abort();
// ~300-600ms later i see a token refresh request from the same process
```

kevin: hmm — that matches a pattern where the request is cancelled but a subsequent response code path (401 -> refresh -> retry) is running in a different microtask and doesn't check the signal. simple fix is to wire the same AbortSignal into the refresh routine so it early-aborts.

ashley: also check http.Agent keepAlive settings. if socket stays open the runtime might dispatch background retries. did you call response.body.cancel() / reader.cancel()?

maria: we just call `res.body?.cancel()` in the streaming wrapper but maybe not in all error paths. good call.

igor: for parity: in python (httpx) context you need to call `await response.aclose()` otherwise background tasks may still complete and trigger refresh. in go, context cancellation often stops the http.Client.Do but you must also ensure you read/close the Body to free goroutines. common leak points across languages.

jon: another wrinkle — our SDK has an internal retry layer that retries idempotent requests on 5xx/401. that layer needs to accept an AbortSignal/Context and propagate it to both the transport and the auth provider. otherwise you can get the scenario: original request aborted -> retry logic kicks in (sees 0 or intermediate state) -> auth refresh -> new request.

kevin: proposed approach:
1) extend AuthProvider.getToken(opts) to accept `{ signal?: AbortSignal }` (TS) / `context.Context` (Go) / `timeout=` (py)
2) propagate the signal/context from the top-level request down into retry/auth layers
3) ensure streaming cancel path closes readers and cancels in-flight auth requests

maria: sounds right. small code sketch for TS: 
```ts
// transport.ts
const ctrl = new AbortController();
const token = await auth.getToken({ signal: ctrl.signal });
const res = await fetch(url, { signal: ctrl.signal, headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` } });
// user abort
ctrl.abort();
// auth.getToken should throw DOMException if aborted and the retry layer should stop
```

ashley: i'll take ownership to add `signal` plumbing in node + browser paths. adding unit tests for abort during token refresh.

igor: i'll add notes to the go SDK: make sure our `auth.Refresh(ctx)` returns quickly on ctx.Done and that caller closes `resp.Body` in all code paths.

sre-jen: FYI might surface as unexpected traffic to identity provider — keep an eye on refresh spikes when you test. i can watch the idp logs when you run the repro. :eyes: 

devex-bot: created issue #4321 — "propagate abort signal to auth provider and close stream on cancellation" (https://github.com/redwood-inference/sdk/issues/4321)

maria: thanks. i'll add a tiny repro in the issue (node stream + rotating refresh) so we can CI test. ping me if you want to pair on the token plumbing.

jon: quick follow-up — for backward compatibility, make the `signal` param optional but document that without it long-running auth refreshes won't be cancelled. otherwise good to go.

ashley: +1. i'll open a draft PR and tag you all.

maria: perfect — closing the loop here. thanks all!
